subject: anaesthesia
title: Spinal Anaesthesia: Anatomy, Hyperbaric Solutions, and Needle Designs

steps.title: Anatomical Layers Traversed
steps.tx: **Anatomical layers traversed in midline spinal puncture** from posterior skin to the subarachnoid space comprise skin, subcutaneous fat, supraspinous ligament (joining spinous process tips), interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum (dense yellow elastin providing characteristic tactile resistance), epidural space containing fat and internal vertebral venous plexus, dura mater, and arachnoid mater.

steps.title: Spinal Cord Termination Levels
steps.tx: **Spinal cord and dural sac anatomical landmarks** establish safety boundaries for needle insertion: the adult spinal cord terminates at the conus medullaris at the lower border of L1 (or upper border of L2), while in full-term neonates it terminates lower at L3. The dural sac extends to S2 in adults (S3 to S4 in infants). Lumbar puncture is performed strictly at or below the L3-L4 interspace to prevent traumatic spinal cord injury.

steps.title: Ligamentum Flavum and Tactile 'Pop'
steps.tx: **Ligamentum flavum tactile resistance** represents the thickest ligament traversed during neuraxial entry, composed of 80 percent elastin fibers running between adjacent laminae. Advancing the spinal or epidural needle produces a characteristic dense gritty resistance, followed by a sudden distinct loss of resistance ('pop') as the bevel pierces the tough ligamentum flavum and enters the epidural space.

steps.title: Hyperbaric versus Isobaric Solutions
steps.tx: **Baricity of intrathecal local anaesthetics** compares solution density against human cerebrospinal fluid (normal CSF density 1.0003 to 1.0008 g/mL at 37 degrees Celsius). Hyperbaric bupivacaine (0.5 percent bupivacaine formulated with 8 percent dextrose, density 1.026) sinks down toward gravitationally dependent areas of the spinal canal, allowing predictable control of sensory block height by tilting the operating table.

steps.title: Controlling Sensory Block Height
steps.tx: **Factors governing spinal sensory block height** divide into drug-related and patient-related factors: the primary determinant of block level is the total mass (dose in milligrams) and baricity of local anaesthetic injected, combined with patient positioning during the initial 15 to 20 minutes (before fixation). Vertebral column curvature (thoracic kyphosis pooling hyperbaric solution at T4 in the supine position) shapes the final dermatomal spread.

steps.title: Cutting versus Pencil-Point Needles
steps.tx: **Spinal needle tip geometry classification** divides into sharp cutting needles and non-cutting pencil-point needles. The traditional Quincke needle features a sharp cutting bevel that slices longitudinally through dural fibers, creating a gaping hole. Pencil-point needles (Whitacre, Sprotte, Pencan) feature a rounded solid tip with a lateral eye, which separates and stretches dural elastic fibers without cutting, reducing post-dural puncture headache rates.

steps.title: Subarachnoid Additives and Opioids
steps.tx: **Intrathecal adjuvants and additive pharmacology** enhance sensory block quality and prolong postoperative analgesia: preservative-free morphine (100 to 200 micrograms) produces up to 18 to 24 hours of profound visceral analgesia via spinal cord substantia gelatinosa mu-opioid receptor binding, but requires respiratory monitoring for delayed central depression at 6 to 12 hours. Lipophilic fentanyl (15 to 25 micrograms) accelerates onset and prolongs analgesia for 2 to 4 hours.

steps.title: Post-Spinal Monitoring and Aftercare
steps.tx: **Subarachnoid block post-procedure care** requires continuous vital sign surveillance: the clinician confirms sensory dermatomal block height using cold ice or pinprick discrimination, verifies motor block using the Bromage score, and monitors non-invasive blood pressure every two to three minutes during the initial 15 minutes to catch sympathetic blockade hypotension.
